111117.etyen:
From Nord-Makedonia (“North Macedonia”) + -sk (“adjective-forming suffix”). The country name is from Nord- (“north”) + Makedonia (“Macedonia”).
The second element is ultimately from Ancient Greek Μᾰκεδονῐ́ᾱ (Măkedonĭ́ā, “Macedonia”), from Μᾰκεδών (Măkedṓn, “a Macedonian”) and the place-name suffix -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā). The ethnonym is traditionally connected with μᾰκεδνός (măkednós, “tall, tapering”); a derivation of that adjective from Pre-Greek has also been proposed.
Parallel formations include Norwegian Nynorsk nordmakedonsk, Danish nordmakedonsk and nordmakedonisk, Swedish nordmakedonsk and nordma

en.g: a male given name from Latin, feminine equivalent Julia and Julie, equivalent to English Julius

1000461.etyen:
Derived from Latin Iūlius (“Roman family name”), of uncertain origin. The Latin name has variously been explained as a contraction of a reconstructed Old Latin personal name meaning “descended from or pertaining to Jove”, or as deriving from Ancient Greek ἴουλος (íoulos, “down; first growth of the beard”); it has also been associated with the mythological Iulus, son of Aeneas. In Norway, the name is first attested in the early 17th century, with the earliest documented use from Hadsel in Nordland.
Compare Danish Julius, Swedish Julius, Faroese Julius, Icelandic Júlíus, German Julius, French Ju

1005069.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse -veri (“inhabitant-forming suffix”). The Old Norse element was used to form names for inhabitants or members of a group, as in Rómverjar (“Romans”).
The element is probably related to var (“wary, cautious”), vare (“to warn, caution”) and verge (“to defend, protect”), but the precise historical formation is uncertain.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk -vær and Icelandic Icelandic -verji (“inhabitant-forming suffix”).
